# Draft:Persecution of Sufis in the Ottoman Empire (1669-1685)

Persecution of Sufis in the Ottoman Empire (1669-1685) occurred during when the Kadizadeli influence was dominant in the courts of the Ottoman Empire and was supported by the Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha and the Sultan Mehmed IV. the Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha had given the Sultan attention of Vani Mehmet Efendi, a Kadizadeli, who he had been railing against Sufi lodges and tombs already.
Background
In the 17th century, there were a lot of changes made to the Ottoman Empire and a lot of reformist groups had popped up. One of these groups was the Kadizadeli, based off of the beliefs of Kadızade Mehmed Effendi,Muhammad Birgivi Effendi, Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya. They had been preaching in mosques, such as Hagia Sophia, during the reign of Sultan Murad IV.
Origins of the Kadizadeli movement
Kadizade Mehmet Efendi, born in 1582 in Balikesir, Ottoman Empire, is an Athari reformist who influenced the government's religious discourse about Sufis in the Ottoman Empire in the 17th century and for decades, his views were followed by the Kadezadelis until the early-mid 18th, when the movement started to die out. Kadizade was influenced by Ibn Taymiyyah and translated his books from Arabic into Turkish. One of these books was "Al Siyasah al Shariyyah." The original translation goes back to Ashiq Pasha, which he translated to the sultan of his time Selim II. Kadizade modified Ashiq Pasha's translation and presented it to Sultan Murad IV.
Kadizade was originally a Sufi, following the Bayrami tariqah, but later renounced Sufism.
In 1633, at the Sultan Ahmed mosque, Kadizade had a confrontation with the Sufi mystic, and his rival, Ebûlhayr Mecdeddin Abdülmecid.
